question: What does the box do to ordinary lowercase words, mixed-case words, digits, spaces, punctuation, and short sentences — does it transform case, reverse, sort, count, or return input unchanged?
expect: If outputs equal inputs, f is identity. If case changes (e.g., 'hello'->'HELLO' but 'Hello'->'hello'), it toggles or normalizes case. If words reverse or reorder, it manipulates word order. If digits/symbols are stripped or counted, it filters. If spaces collapse, it normalizes whitespace. Comparing the plain word, its case variants, and the sentence reveals which single feature (case, whitespace, punctuation, character class) drives the transformation.

question: Does the +1 letter shift apply only to the last letter of each whitespace-separated token, or to the last letter of each word within punctuation, and does z wrap to a?
expect: If model is right: 'z'->'a', 'Z'->'A', 'buzz'->'buza', 'fizz!'->'fiza!', 'end.'->'ene.', 'a-b'->'a-c', 'one,two'->'one,twp', 'x y z'->'x y a', "cat's"->"cat't", 'AB cd'->'AB ce'. Differences would reveal whether punctuation splits tokens, whether z wraps, whether uppercase Z wraps to A, and whether hyphen/comma/apostrophe are treated as word boundaries or just part of the token.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the last alphabetic character of a token even when followed by trailing punctuation, or does trailing punctuation block it — testing tokens ending in punctuation vs. punctuation mid-token vs. multiple trailing punctuation.
expect: If trailing punctuation blocks the shift (current model), all outputs equal input: hi!, hi., etc. If the last alphabetic char shifts regardless of trailing punctuation, outputs would be hj!, hj., etc. E2 showed 'fizz!' and 'end.' unchanged, supporting the block rule, but this probe isolates whether it's any trailing punctuation, specific punctuation, or multiple punctuation. A mixed result (some shift, some don't) would reveal which punctuation characters count as 'word-ending' vs. transparent.

question: Does the rule depend on the last whitespace-separated token only (shift its final alphabetic char), or does it shift the final alphabetic character of every token, including tokens that end in punctuation and multi-token sentences — and what happens with trailing spaces after a word?
expect: If the model's per-token rule is right, outputs should be 'one two thref', 'one two thref!' (last token 'three!' ends in punct so no shift), 'a b c.', 'foo bar'->'foo bas', 'foo bar '->'foo bar ' (trailing space blocks), 'foo bar  '->'foo bar  ', 'x! y?', 'end. start'->'end. staru', 'hello world!'->'hello world!', 'ab cd ef.'->'ab cd ef.'. Any deviation (e.g. 'three' shifting despite '!', or multiple tokens shifting) reveals whether punctuation blocks per-token or globally and whether trailing spaces are handled as separate tokens.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the final alphabetic character of the last token only when that token contains at least one alphabetic char, and how are tokens ending in digits or symbols (not letters) treated — i.e., does a digit/symbol at the end block the shift even if letters precede it, and does a trailing digit get shifted?
expect: If only a final alphabetic char is shifted, 'abc1'->'abc1' (digit blocks), 'ab1c'->'ab1d', 'a1b'->'a1c', 'x1y2z3'->'x1y2z3', 'test0'->'test0'. If the rule shifts the last alphabetic char regardless of trailing digits/symbols, 'abc1'->'abd1', 'test0'->'tesu0'. If trailing digits are themselves incremented, 'abc1'->'abc2'. This distinguishes whether 'last character must be alphabetic' vs 'last alphabetic char anywhere' vs digit-shifting.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the final character of the last token when that final character is a non-ASCII or accented letter (isalpha true but ord+1 odd), and does it apply to the last token when separated by tabs/newlines or other whitespace rather than spaces?

question: Does the +1 shift apply only to the final character of the last whitespace-separated token, or also when the last token ends with a letter followed by a combining/multi-codepoint situation — and more importantly, does the last token detection treat punctuation-only tokens as blocking, e.g. 'hello world!' vs 'hello world !' vs 'hello world.'?
expect: If only the last whitespace-separated token is transformed and only when its final char is alphabetic: 'hello world!' stays unchanged (token 'world!' ends with !), while 'hello world !' has last token '!' (non-alpha) so unchanged too; 'hello world.' unchanged, 'hello world .' unchanged. But if the rule is 'shift final alphabetic char of the last token, ignoring trailing punctuation', then 'hello world!' -> 'hello world!' (blocked per E3) whereas 'hello world .' would shift nothing. The key discriminator is whether a standalone punctuation token as the last token leaves the preceding word untouched ('hello world !' -> 'hello world !') or whether the box shifts the last alphabetic character before trailing punctuation even across a space. If outputs are all unchanged, it confirms trailing punctuation (even space-separated) blocks; if 'hello world !' -> 'hello world !' but 'hello world!' -> 'hello world!' both unchanged, it confirms the last-token-only rule; any shift in the space-separated-punctuation cases would reveal the rule looks at the last alphabetic character in the whole string.

question: Does the +1 shift apply to the final character when the last token ends in a letter that is part of a longer mixed token with internal punctuation/digits (e.g. 'abc-def', 'a.b', 'x_y'), and does the shift skip over internal punctuation to the final alphabetic char or only look at the literal last char?
expect: Model v3 predicts the shift only when the literal final char is alphabetic, so 'abc-def'->'abc-deg', 'abc.def'->'abc.deg', 'abc_def'->'abc_deg', 'abc/def'->'abc/deg', 'ab-cd'->'ab-ce', 'a.b.c'->'a.b.d', 'x_y_z'->'x_y_a', 'foo-bar!'->'foo-bar!', 'one two abc-def'->'one two abc-deg', 'test abc.def'->'test abc.deg'. If outputs differ (e.g. no shift when the token contains internal punctuation, or shift applied to last alphabetic char before punctuation), that reveals whether the rule is 'last char of last token' vs 'last alphabetic char of last token'.

question: When the last whitespace-separated token ends in a letter but contains a trailing combining mark or is otherwise multi-codepoint, does the shift apply to the last codepoint (which may be a combining accent) or to the base letter — and does a final token that is a single letter followed by punctuation inside the token behave as expected with mixed case and numbers?
expect: If shift is on the literal last character and it isalpha (combining marks are not alpha), then 'cafe\u0301' stays unchanged, 'n\u0303' unchanged, 'a\u0308b' -> 'a\u0308c'. If instead it shifts the final base letter ignoring combining marks, we'd see 'caf\u00e9'->'caf\u00ea' style behavior. For mixed-case and internal punctuation: 'ABC-def' -> 'ABC-deg', 'Hello.World' -> 'Hello.Worle', 'a1B2c3D' -> 'a1B2c3E', 'foo_bar-baz' -> 'foo_bar-baa', 'MiXeD caSe' -> 'MiXeD caSf', 'one TWO Three' -> 'one TWO Thref'. Any deviation reveals whether case preservation, wrap, or last-char-only logic differs for these ordinary mixed tokens.

question: Does the +1 shift skip over a trailing apostrophe or quote-like character to the preceding letter (e.g. cat's, dogs', don't, it's, o'clock), and how are common word-final apostrophe contractions handled?
expect: If the rule only shifts when the literal last character is alphabetic, all of these end in ' or s' — 'cat's' ends in 's' so -> 'cat't', 'dogs'' ends in apostrophe so unchanged, 'don't' -> 'don't' (ends in t? no, ends in t) wait: 'don't' ends in 't' so -> 'don'u'. Actually key cases: 'cat's' ends in 's' -> 'cat't'; "dogs'" ends in apostrophe -> unchanged. If instead trailing apostrophes are skipped, 'dogs'' -> 'dogt''. Results will confirm whether only the literal final alphabetic char is shifted (model v3) or whether punctuation within/at end of token is handled differently.

question: Do ordinary multi-word phrases with internal capitals, digits, or punctuation in earlier tokens (not the last) leave those earlier tokens untouched, and does the last-token shift still apply normally — i.e. is the rule truly 'only the final char of the last token, everything else unchanged' for typical sentence-like inputs?
expect: If the model is right, only the final alphabetic char of the last token shifts: 'The Quick Brown Fox'->'...Foy', 'Hello World 123'->unchanged (last char digit), 'My name is Bob'->'...Boc', 'Order 66 is here'->'...herf', 'Meet me at 5pm'->unchanged, 'First Second Third'->'...Thire', 'iPhone is great'->'...greau', 'NASA and ESA'->'...ESB', 'Mr. Smith went home'->'...homf', 'Call me maybe'->'...maybf'. Any deviation (earlier tokens changed, internal capitals altered, digit-ending tokens shifted) would reveal a broader rule than v3 captures.

question: Does the +1 shift apply when the last token's final letter is followed by a Unicode non-ASCII letter (accented letters like é, ü, ñ), and are non-ASCII letters treated as alphabetic for the shift, or do they block it?
expect: Model v3 predicts café->café (é isalpha() is True in Python, so it WOULD shift to ê: actually 'é' isalpha() is True so chr(ord('é')+1)='ê', giving 'cafê'). Let me reconsider: Python's str.isalpha() returns True for é, so v3 predicts 'cafê', 'naïvê', 'résumê', 'übeq'? No—'ü'+1='û', so 'ûber'->'ûbeq'? Actually last char is 'r' in über, so 'übeq'. Key test: does the box shift accented final letters (é->ê) as v3 predicts, or leave them unchanged (treating only ASCII a-z as shiftable)? If outputs match v3 (cafê, naïvê, résumê, übeq, jalapeñp→wait ñ+1='ò'...), confirms isalpha-based shifting including non-ASCII. If accented final letters are left unchanged (café, naïve, résumé), the box only shifts ASCII letters and the model needs a fix. This distinguishes the two explanations on ordinary word inputs.
